title: Classification / Odd One Out
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Grouping words by a shared property and spotting the one that does not belong

introduction.overview: A classification question gives four or five words (or items) and asks you to pick the one that does not belong with the others. Three or four of the words share a property such as being a fruit, a mammal, a metal or a language; the odd one lacks that property. The task is to discover the shared property quickly and precisely. This chapter focuses on words; the next chapter covers numbers and letters.
introduction.placementRelevance: Classification questions are commonly asked in the reasoning section of company aptitude rounds. They are easy marks for students who build the habit of naming the common property before choosing.
introduction.realWorldContext: Sorting items in a shop, filing documents into folders and tagging products in an online catalogue all rely on classification.

learningObjectives: Identify the common property shared by a group of words
Distinguish between a category and an exception within it
Handle questions where more than one property fits, by choosing the most specific one
Classify items by use, origin, state, shape and unit
Avoid being misled by words that look similar

requiredTopics: Basic general knowledge of animals, plants, materials and units
prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Common groupings: fruits and vegetables; mammals, birds, reptiles and fish; metals and non-metals; 2D and 3D shapes; units of length, mass and volume; languages and programming languages.

coreDefinitions: Classification: the process of placing items into groups according to a shared property.
Common property: the attribute that three or four of the items share (for example "all are mammals").
Odd one out: the item that does not have the common property.
Category and exception: a category is the set of items with the property; an exception is an item that fails the property test.
Specific property: the narrowest property shared by the majority; it is usually the intended one.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every odd-one-out question has exactly one intended property. Your job is to name it. A good habit is to find two of the items that obviously belong together, name what they share, and then check whether the remaining items share it.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Picture four boxes of labels. If three words fit under the label "birds" and the fourth fits under "mammals", the fourth is odd. If more than one label fits, choose the label that fits the largest group of items most precisely.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Step 1: pair up
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Find the two most obviously related words
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Start where the relationship is strongest.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Step 2: name the property
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Write the property in one phrase
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: When several properties seem to fit.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Step 3: test the rest
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Check the other items against the property
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The item that fails is the answer.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Sparrow is a bird → odd one out

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Common classes
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Mammals, birds, fish, reptiles; metals, non-metals; length, mass, volume; 2D, 3D
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Litre is a unit of volume; the others are units of length

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Specificity rule
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If two properties fit, choose the one shared by more items
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Iron, Copper, Gold, Diamond → three metals, one non-metal

mainNarrative: Read all the words once before deciding. Many mistakes come from stopping at the first two words and forming a wrong idea of the property. The correct property must hold for all items except one.

Think of several properties for each word: what it is (category), where it lives or is used (habitat or function), what it is made of, what it measures, how it looks. For Mercury, Venus, Moon and Mars the property "planets" covers three; the Moon is a satellite, so it is the odd one out.

When a word belongs to more than one class (a bat is a mammal that flies), look for the property that separates the odd item most cleanly. In Eagle, Parrot, Bat and Crow, "birds" fits three and Bat is the mammal. "Flying animals" would fit all four, so it is not the intended property.

Unit and measurement questions are common: in Kilometre, Litre, Metre and Centimetre, three measure length, so Litre (volume) is the odd one. In Kilogram, Metre, Second and Newton, the first three are base units while Newton is derived.

deepDiveAspects.title: Two plausible answers
deepDiveAspects.content: If you find two words that could both be odd, step back and name the properties. The better answer usually has the property that fits exactly three other words, with a clear reason why the odd word fails.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why general knowledge matters
deepDiveAspects.content: Classification questions use ordinary facts: whale and dolphin are mammals, shark is a fish, diamond is a form of carbon and not a metal. Reading widely helps more than memorising any rule.

solvedExamples.title: Animals
solvedExamples.question: Find the odd one out: Dog, Cat, Sparrow, Cow
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Name the property shared by three items.

steps.title: Test the others
steps.explanation: Cow is a mammal. Sparrow is a bird.

steps.title: Choose
steps.explanation: Sparrow does not share the property.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Three are mammals and one is a bird.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Selecting Cow because it is not a pet.

solvedExamples.title: Units
solvedExamples.question: Find the odd one out: Kilometre, Litre, Metre, Centimetre

steps.title: List what each measures
steps.explanation: Kilometre: length. Litre: volume. Metre: length. Centimetre: length.

steps.title: Choose
steps.explanation: Litre is a unit of volume.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The group property is "unit of length".
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing Centimetre because it is the smallest.

solvedExamples.title: Sub-classes
solvedExamples.question: Find the odd one out: Whale, Shark, Dolphin, Seal
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: All live in water, so look for a finer property.

steps.title: Try "live in water"
steps.explanation: All four live in water, so this property cannot separate them.

steps.title: Try "mammals"
steps.explanation: Whale, Dolphin and Seal are mammals.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A property that fits every item cannot make one odd; a finer property is needed.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Stopping at "sea animals" and finding no odd one.

shortcutMethods.title: Name-the-property method

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Compare every item with every other item.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Find the two closest words, name their property, and test the remaining words against it. One test per word is enough.

rulesForApplication: If every word fits your property, the property is too broad; narrow it down.
Prefer properties that separate three words from one.
Check units, states and categories first in science-related questions.
Do not choose based on spelling or length of the word unless all other properties fail.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a property that fits all items
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Choosing a broad label such as "animals".
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Narrow it down until exactly one item fails.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing based on a rare property
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Picking the item that is not a pet, not red, not large.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Choose the scientific or functional property.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Forming the property from the first two items.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Cross out the two words that clearly belong together, then test the other two against their property.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: These are quick questions; if the property is not clear in 20 seconds, skip.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The best preparation is general awareness: units, categories of animals, materials, instruments.

summaryBullets: The property must fit all but one item.
Narrow a property that fits everything.
Check units, categories, states and functions.

keyTakeaways: Always state the property in words.
General knowledge is the real preparation.
Do not choose on appearance alone.
selfCheckQuestions: Can I say what property Iron, Copper and Gold share, and why Diamond is out?
Can I explain why Bat is the odd one in Eagle, Parrot, Bat, Crow?
Can I separate base units from derived units?
